item.title: Giants to place KR/WR Braxton Berrios on IR, per report
item.description: Giants’ wide receiver depth takes another hit.
item.content:encoded:
Braxton Berrios is being placed on injured reserve by the New York Giants after suffering a foot injury in Sunday’s 36-24 victory over the Arizona Cardinals, according to a report from ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter.

It is unclear when Berrios was injured, though his last play was a late-second quarter punt return on which he lost 2 yards.

Berrios was just added to the 53-man roster last week after the Giants released Odell Beckham Jr. Considering Beckham’s weekend rant after his release, he may have taken himself out of the running for a return to the Giants.

The Giants have wide receivers Dalen Cambre and Jalin Hyatt on the practice squad. They cut ties with veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton, now a member of the Indianapolis Colts, early in the season.

Berrios has returned five kickoffs for an average of 27.6 yards and four punts for an average of 2.5 yards this season.

Charlie Jones, an experienced NFL kick returner, replaced Berrios on kickoff returns Sunday. He averaged 23.0 yards on three returns. He took over for Berrios on punt returns after the injury, averaging 14.5 yards on two returns.

item.title: Donovan Jackson out with torn meniscus, Christian Darrisaw in concussion protocol
item.description: The Vikings remain undefeated at 4-0, but they will have to deal with some injuries along their offensive line.
item.content:encoded:
The Vikings remain undefeated at 4-0, but they will have to deal with some injuries along their offensive line.

Head coach Kevin O'Connell told reporters in his Monday press conference that left guard Donovan Jackson suffered a torn meniscus and will likely miss the rest of the regular season.

Jackson is set to undergo surgery to repair the injury.

O'Connell also noted that left tackle Christian Darrisaw is in the concussion protocol after Sunday's win over Miami.

But tight end Ben Yurosek and offensive lineman Michael Jurgens are set to return to practice this week. Both players are currying on injured reserve.

The Vikings will be on the road to play the Saints on Sunday.

item.title: Mike Vrabel: Efton Chism III has earned more opportunities
item.description: On Sunday, OBJ met EC3.
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, OBJ met EC3. And the stellar, game-winning catch made by Patriots receiver Efton Chism III will result in more chances to make more next-level grabs.

"Sure, of course," coach Mike Vrabel told reporters on Monday regarding whether Chism has earned more opportunities. "That's what happens. I mean, guys continue to take advantage of their opportunities, they get more opportunities. I mean, we've been finding ways to work Chis in there previously. And it's a balance, but he certainly did a lot of things well. I know that he'll continue to do things well for us and continue to know a bunch of different spots."

On Sunday, Chism was on the field for 34 offensive snaps. Targeted four times, he had two catches for 42 yards, including the 23-yard clincher.

In Week 1 against the Seahawks, Chism was inactive. In Week 2 vs. the Steelers, Chism had 10 snaps; he was targeted once, for minus-2 yards. In Week 3 at the Jaguars, Chism had 16 snaps. He had one catch on two targets, for one yard.

So he has already been earning more work, one game at a time. And it looks like Chism will get even more.

Which means that, contrary to the prediction from Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson, we probably willhear from him again.

item.title: Cowboys guard Tyler Smith has real chance to play Thursday night
item.description: Tyler Smith may play this week for the Cowboys
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys could be getting a very important player back this week. Dallas just won on the road against the Houston Texans and will host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Thursday night. No rest for the weary.

Someone who has had some rest seems to stand a chance to play, though. Stephen Jones hinted on Monday during his appearance on 105.3 The Fan that Tyler Smith may suit up and be in action.

Smith has been on injured reserve since the season began due to a thumb injury. While T.J. Bass has heroically held it down in his absence, Smith is arguably the best interior lineman in the NFL. Him returning would significantly boost what is already a very good offense.

As Smith was on IR he had to miss at least four games and obviously the fourth has just passed. ESPN’s Todd Archer noted earlier in the day on Monday that he was going to have his practice window opened, but the Stephen quote took things to another level.

It goes without saying that this would be a huge boost for Dallas as noted. We will see.

item.content:encoded:
Another NFL Sunday is in the books, with the Atlanta Falcons and New Orleans Saints still in the queue for "Monday Night Football" to close out Week 4.

The day offered plenty of exciting matchups, including a thriller between the Dallas Cowboys and Houston Texans that saw Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb connect for the go-ahead touchdown with just 0:43 on the clock. It also offered plenty of injuries that NFL fans and fantasy football managers alike will be keeping a close eye on in the week to come.

Several stars went down with injuries, headlined by Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson, who left the stadium in a walking boot after suffering an ankle injury in Sunday's win over the Tennessee Titans. Jackson is expected to undergo an MRI on Monday, per reports.

Running back Saquon Barkley exited Week 4 with a hamstring injury, while Ja'Marr Chase was ruled out with a concussion after having his facemask grabbed before getting tackled by a defender.

The Kansas City Chiefs lost two of their top receivers, too, as Rashee Rice went down with a hamstring issue and Tyquan Thornton suffered a gruesome ankle injury that seems likely to have ended his season. Per The Athletic's Michael Silver, the team has reached out to Tyreek Hill's agent about a possible reunion.

item.title: Travis Glover passes the test in first significant playing time since 2024
item.description: The Packers’ latest experiment at right guard made the grade.
item.content:encoded:
After upending their offensive line over the post-Thursday Night Football mini bye, the Packers coaching staff reached into a hat and pulled out a new name to start at right guard for Sunday’s game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Instead of Kevin Zeitler or Donovan Jennings or Jacob Monk or Jager Burton, it was Travis Glover getting the nod between Sean Rhyan and Anthony Belton.

A 2024 sixth round pick, we haven’t seen Glover on the field for a game that matters in quite some time. The last time he made an appearance was in the Packers’ loss to the eventual Super Bowl champion Philadelphia Eagles, when he came in at left guard in relief of an injured Elgton Jenkins, who dropped out after just four plays. Facing off against a ferocious Philadelphia front, Glover was penalized three times before he was ultimately benched in favor of Kadeem Telfort. However, after an injury to starting center Josh Myers forced Sean Rhyan to take over at center, Glover got back into the game at right guard. 

All told, he played 33 snaps and had a dreadful day, posting a pass blocking grade of just 1.8 according to Pro Football Focus. For comparison, Donovan Jennings and Jacob Monk put up  pass blocking grades of 40.0 and 48.2, respectively, in the Packers’ Week 1 loss to the Vikings this season, and that was one of the single-worst blocking performances we’ve ever seen. You can and should take PFF grades with a grain of salt, but that’s a startling difference.

Glover missed all of the 2025 season with a back injury, but was back in action this preseason lining up primarily but not exclusively at right tackle. He played 39 snaps on the outside against just 28 at right guard, but with Jennings struggling, Monk unavailable due to injury, and Burton’s experience coming primarily at right guard, those 28 snaps apparently represented enough time on task to give Glover the start.

How did Glover do? It wasn’t a spectacular day for the Packers on the ground or through the air, but Glover came close to achieving a lineman’s ideal day: by and large, he was seen but not heard.

In 60 snaps of work, surrendered just one pressure and was penalized one time, a holding penalty on the Packers’ first offensive play of the fourth quarter. A 19-yard completion to Jonnu Smith on the next play erased that penalty and then some, though, so ultimately it was of little consequence.

Pro Football Focus gave Glover a 59.4 grade overall, bolstered mainly by his 71.4 grade as a pass blocker (they gave him a 53.8 grade for his run blocking). That aligns well with the eye test of the Packers’ offensive line as a whole; by and large, they did a good job protecting Jordan Love but struggled to get much push in the ground game.

It wasn’t necessarily Glover’s fault, but you can see some of the struggles the Packers had on the ground in a 2nd and 3 play in the second quarter. Jordan Morgan gives up ground to Buccaneers’ defensive lineman Rakeem Nunez-Roches so quickly that Glover, coming right to left as a pulling guard, ends up smacking Morgan in the face. For a second, it looks like Glover and Morgan are giving each other a hug as Nunez-Roches takes Kaleb Johnson down for a two-yard loss.

But in a game where the Packers’ offensive line looked relatively competent, especially compared to the rest of the season, Glover, at the very least, was not obviously bad. That’s a step in the right direction.

And hopefully, it’ll be the last the Packers see of him for a while. It was probably unrealistic to expect newly arrived Kevin Zeitler in the lineup this week, but going forward, he’ll hopefully be ready to go. Whatever workouts he’s been doing on his own were almost assuredly not enough to get him from “active, but sitting at home” to “ready to play in an NFL game” in roughly three days of practice, one of which would have been at walkthrough speed. He was always going to need some time, and hopefully another week will do it. 

But if he can’t go, the Packers should at least feel good putting Glover out there again. He wasn’t a clear detriment to the team’s performance, and given what we’ve seen from his teammates this year, that’s a huge compliment.

item.title: Rams boast elite defensive stats even without Myles Garrett
item.description: L.A.’s defense should be even better when starters return from injury
item.content:encoded:
The addition of Trent McDuffie in the offseason is already paying off dividends for the L.A. Rams defense, as they rank second in passing yards allowed, second in yards per pass allowed, and third in EPA per pass allowed through four weeks. Even with no contributions yet from Myles Garrett, or practically Aaron Donald, the Rams have received the pass defensive improvements that they desperately wanted to see from last season.

Now imagine how the defense could do with Garrett, Donald, and Jaylen Watson.

Trent McDuffie is worth it

The Rams traded a late first-round pick in 2026 for McDuffie and then paid him over $30 million per season. This was all in an effort to replace the likes of Darious Williams and company and it’s paying off. McDuffie is arguably the best cornerback in the NFL this season.

The Rams wanted to pair McDuffie with former Chiefs teammate Jaylen Watson, but Watson missed Week 4’s win over the Eagles with a shoulder injury.

And the Rams held Philadelphia to 68 net passing yards.

It certainly helps that Jalen Hurts didn’t have Devonta Smith to throw to this week, but Darius Cooper certainly earned some respect with his two touchdown catches against L.A.‘s defense. It took practically all he had for the first one to be completed, so credit to him for that.

But even so, the Rams held the Eagles to 68 passing yards with Josh Wallace starting and playing the entire game. Wallace certainly deserves more credit too: Going into Week 4, Wallace has been allowing a passer rating of 34.8 on throws in his direction.

4 games, 582 passing yards

The Rams have only allowed 582 passing yards in four games, including a season-worst 205 passing yards against the 49ers in Week 1. Only the Seahawks and Rams have held all four opponents to 205 passing yards or fewer this season.

L.A.’s defense is second in total yards per play allowed at 4.2, also behind Seattle.

One area the Rams would like to improve is forcing more turnovers, as they only have three takeaways and have yet to recover a fumble. This is at least partly related to L.A. only having three sacks and a 19% pressure rate. By comparison, the Vikings have a 36% pressure rate.

This is what Garrett was traded to help with and he has missed the last three games. He didn’t do anything in Week 1. But nobody expects Garrett to miss the entire season and his presence will change everything about the Rams’ front seven.

Per Next Gen Stats, the Rams are averaging 3.1 yards of separation between the defense and the intended receivers of the offense. That ranks as the third-best in the NFL.

Again, this highlights how sticky McDuffie and company have been in coverage this season, a major improvement from 2025.

Rams have more on the way

Garrett has to miss at least this week’s game against the Bills, and then he will be eligible to come off of IR in Week 6. However, the Rams have not indicated that they expect Garrett to return that soon.

If Garrett misses the Cardinals and Raiders games, which would mean six weeks off, he’d return against the Chargers on November 1.

Watson missed this week’s game, but McVay said that it wasn’t even up for discussion that Watson would go on IR, implying that he could return in the next two weeks.

The Rams are reportedly “optimistic” that Donald will return from a back injury in Week 5, according to Mike Garafolo.

Kam Kinchens returned from a hamstring injury in Week 4 and played in 70% of the snaps. This is actually typical for Kinchens, but perhaps he’d be even better next week.

Overall, if the Rams had this defense and only this defense, their prospects for the upcoming schedule would already be fairly good relative to other teams.

However, imagine if this was the Rams defense and then they traded for Myles Garrett, Jaylen Watson, and Aaron Donald between Weeks 5-8.

That’s kind of what could happen. And as long as the rest of the team, and McDuffie, stays on track, that could mean that the L.A. Rams’ defense is as good as we thought it could be after the offseason they used toiling to make it better.

item.title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Colts’ performances from Week 4 London win across the pond
item.description: Ah-hoo, Colts won in London! It was a sloppy start, but the Colts eventually took control. Here’s some individual highlights from Sunday’s win!
item.content:encoded:
After an initial sloppy start, the Indianapolis Colts (2-2) righted the trolleybus offensively, took advantage of a rookie 3rd-string quarterback defensively, and bested the Washington Commanders (1-3), 30-13, in London this past Sunday—now back to playing .500 football for the first time this season.

We’ll look at some of the studs, duds, and maybe a little in between regarding their latest international win:

Horsepower

  • RB Jonathan Taylor: The Colts star workhorse continues to shine overseas, recording 95 total rushing yards and 2 rushing touchdowns on 20 carries (4.8 ypc. avg.). With starting quarterback Daniel Jones clearly shaky play early on (which we’ll get to here in a bit), the Colts went “back to the basics,” and that was riding the efficient Taylor in this one (with some rookie rusher Seth McGowan sprinkled in as a change-of-pace back). Taylor is now the all-time international leading rusher (6 touchdowns) and rushing yards leader (408) in league history, and whether it was “drinking tea” or “waving like the queen” following his two touchdowns runs on the day, he celebrated in London style.
  • DT DeForest Buckner: With the Colts offense spiraling early on (with a fumble lost, three straight punts, and an interception on their first five offensive drives), Buckner, to me, almost single-handedly kept the Colts in this football game defensively with his hustle, impact, and leadership. Whether it was stopping the run, creating pass pressure, or just all-out effort, Buckner played like a man on a mission, and was a huge reason why the Indianapolis defense held the Commanders to just two field goals on their first two offensive drives, despite being gifted a short field on their first possession because of the weird Jones’ fumble. Buckner deserves to be a Colts’ Ring of Honor player when it’s all said-and-done, and his collective impact on Sunday is a big reason why. That was a performance to remember, one day looking back at his standout career here in Indianapolis. While we’re on the position, I’d also like to give backup defensive tackle Ade Adebawore an honorable mention, who made his pass rushing presence felt in limited action again, with 0.5 sacks and 2 QB hits. He continues to be a menace as a subpackage interior pass rusher.
  • LB Jaylon Carlies: The Colts much maligned starting linebacker unit has taken its fair share of lumps and growing criticism to begin the 2026 campaign, but arguably had their best performance of the season on Sunday. In particular, Carlies showcased his best, and elite athleticism, by somehow batting an Athan Kaliakmanis pass to himself for the interception early in the 3rd quarter.
  • CB Charvarius Ward: The Colts secondary had its fair share of coverage gaffes, by allowing a handful of explosive big plays to the rookie Kaliakmanis, but wearing the guardians cap again, Ward arguably had his best game of the season in coverage. Specifically, he allowed just two receptions for 13 total receiving yards on 7 targets in coverage (28.6 catch rate) with 3 pass breakups.
  • PK Spencer Shrader: Regarding what was a narrowly won offseason competition, the Colts absolutely made the right call by naming Shrader the victor, who was a perfect 3 for 3 from field goal range again including makes from 48 yards, 52 yards, and 44 yards. That’ll certainly play on special teams!

Horseplay

  • QB Daniel Jones: For the first 1.5 quarters in this one, Jones looked like how a lot of Colts fans may have thought he’d look coming off last year’s season-ending torn Achilles in Week 14 with no preseason reps. He has to take better care of the football on the weird sack fumble, and the interception off his back-foot under duress to Commanders veteran cornerback Rasul Douglas is just a play that can’t happen at this level. Jones has to either feel the pressure earlier or “eat the sack,” rather than throw a gifted lollipop in coverage. Jones looked closer to the failed franchise quarterback hopeful who was too turnover prone with the New York Giants than the breakout quarterback we surprisingly saw during the first half of last season in his Indianapolis debut. No idea if the Colts coaching staff was ever seriously contemplating an in-game change, but one more offensive drive that ended in another Jones brutal turnover, and as fans, we were realistically getting close to advocating for seeing Anthony Richardson again—if we weren’t already. Jones absolutely cannot play that way again in Pittsburgh next week, which has been a historical franchise house of horrors.
  • CB Sauce Gardner: Whether you want to argue that Gardner has not lived up to his billing so far in Indianapolis, after the Colts surprisingly surrendered two first round picks, it’s fair game—although Gardner himself did not make that trade. In London, he clearly played his worst game as a member of the Colts. He allowed 4 receptions for 117 total receiving yards and a touchdown reception on his 5 pass coverage targets, although I will also contend that his safety help (i.e., rookie A.J. Haulcy) and the Indy pass pressure didn’t do him favors either by leaving him on a coverage island for so long. Even with his lack of interceptions, the Colts need Gardner to be a shutdown #1 cornerback, and on Sunday, he was far from it, as he was openly picked on by Kaliakmanis on two explosive passing plays deep.

item.title: Colts Monday Morning Awards: Week 4 vs Commanders (London)
item.description: The Colts shook off an ugly first quarter and leaned on their run game to walk out of Tottenham Hotspur Stadium with a convincing 30-13 win. Was the first month of the season pretty? Absolutely not, but the Stampede Blue Community would have taken a 2-2 record after a tough stretch against the Ravens, Chiefs, […]
item.content:encoded:
The Colts shook off an ugly first quarter and leaned on their run game to walk out of Tottenham Hotspur Stadium with a convincing 30-13 win.

Was the first month of the season pretty? Absolutely not, but the Stampede Blue Community would have taken a 2-2 record after a tough stretch against the Ravens, Chiefs, Texans and Commanders, in that order. The defense has stepped up in consecutive games and dominated third down, while the rushing attack took over and Jonathan Taylor continued cementing his name into the record books as an international superstar. 

Here’s to a new edition of Monday Morning Awards.

MVP of the Game: Jonathan Taylor

Who else deserves it other than the best player on the roster? Taylor rushed for 95 yards and two touchdowns on 20 carries, becoming both the NFL’s all-time leading rusher and scorer in international games. After he bounced left for a 5-yard score to give the Colts a lead they would never relinquish, he celebrated his sixth touchdown of the season by sitting criss-cross applesauce to veritably sip tea in front of a roaring crowd in London.

With 75 career touchdowns, Indy’s 27-year-old tailback joined Emmitt Smith, LaDainian Tomlinson, and Jim Brown as the only running backs to reach that mark before turning 28. Taylor doesn’t turn 28 until after the regular season and wild-card weekend ends. 

Dud of the Game: Daniel Jones performance

The dud of the game came from Daniel Jones, who was strip-sacked by Odafe Oweh and lost the fumble, giving Washington the ball near the Colts’ red zone on the second snap from scrimmage. Jones later threw an interception off his back foot to cornerback Rasul Douglas, marking his eighth turnover-worthy play through four games and putting the Colts in a 6-0 hole before he finally settled in. The veteran QB finished 19 of 34 for just 143 passing yards, but scrambled for a 4-yard touchdown to put the Colts ahead by two scores early in the fourth quarter.

Worst Play of the Game: Turnover terminates opening drive

The worst play of the game has to be the opening sequence as the Colts had the ball for just two snaps before Jones fumbled and gave Washington a chance to seize an early lead on a short field. Oweh rushed from the right edge and drove left tackle Bernhard Raimann straight into Jones’ dropback, which knocked the ball loose before Oweh recovered it himself.

Best Play of the Game: Jaylon Carlies’ interception

If the firs half was hard to stomach, any doubts of leaving London with a victory were halted when the defense finally got the big turnover it needed to start the third quarter. Washington was pushed backward from a penalty and faced with third-and-17, then linebacker Jaylon Carlies reached up to haul in a pass intended for Andrew Williams for his first career interception and returned it to the Commanders’ 27-yard line. Four plays later, Taylor plunged into the end zone and gave the Colts a 17-6 lead.

Best Position Group: Defensive line

The defensive front combined for 14 stops and 11 QB hits, then made life miserable as Washington was able to convert just 2-of-15 third downs. Laiatu Latu and Adetomiwa Adebawore combined for a sack that knocked opposing starter Marcus Mariota out of the game, while Latu added two more quarterback hits. DeForest Buckner had three quarterback hits of his own, and collected his 100th career tackle for loss. The biggest difference was the pressure as Washington could not move the sticks with its emergency third-string QB. 

Unsung Hero: Spencer Shrader

Kicker Spencer Shrader made all three field goals from 48, 52, and 44-yards out to keep the Colts ahead with enough cushion to maintain a lead. His 52-yarder in the third quarter pushed the Colts’ lead back to seven after Washington had trimmed the deficit to 17-13.

Shrader quietly put together one of those games where you don’t notice the kicker until you look at the scoreboard and realize he has as many points as the opponent. Along with three extra points, Shrader collected 12 points while the Commanders left 13 on the scoreboard. 

Rookie of the Week: Seth McGowan

Rookie running back Seth McGowan didn’t need a huge workload, but his 10 touches were more than enough to make an impact. With Taylor doing most of the heavy-lifting, McGowan carried the ball six times for 31 yards, averaging 5.2 per carry. Two of those six carries resulted in first downs as McGowan provided a nice change of pace and showed why he’s capable of getting more opportunities. McGowan also returned four kickoffs for a combined 102 return yards, with the final return stopping the Commanders’ momentum and ultimately led to a field goal. 

Honorable Mention: Justin Walley

Sunday was Justin Walley’s best game of his young career. He finished with eight tackles and a key sack on an blitz that forced a fourth down and knocked the Commanders out of field-goal range. Walley came screaming uncovered from the blindside and dropped Kaliakmanis for a 9-yard sack that forced Washington to punt. Walley posted a 75.4 coverage grade, which ranked among the top 10 cornerbacks who played at least 10 coverage snaps in Week 4.

Charvarius Ward deserves credit when its due, too. Washington completed only one pass against him on five targets, while Ward recorded three forced incompletions. His three forced incompletions and 41.0 snaps per reception was third among cornerbacks through Sunday in Week 4. 

Indy struggled to start the game, but played complementary football in the second half. The Colts finished with just one penalty compared to Washington’s 10 and won the turnover battle after the early mistake. Between the clean play, dominance on third down and pounding the rock with their marquee tailback, the Colts stuck to their playstyle and return stateside with an even 2-2 record. 

The Colts travel to Pittsburgh to face the Steelers (2-2) next Sunday, with kickoff set for 1 p.m.

item.title: Five Plays: NC State First Quarter
item.description: Louisville lost another football game on Saturday. They also lost another game that they should have won. Penalties had been a major issue for this team, but they replaced that issue with turnovers this time around. But the biggest issue remains, and that issue is blown coverages by the secondary. For the second straight week, […]
item.content:encoded:
Louisville lost another football game on Saturday. They also lost another game that they should have won. Penalties had been a major issue for this team, but they replaced that issue with turnovers this time around. But the biggest issue remains, and that issue is blown coverages by the secondary. For the second straight week, they turned a ball control offense into an explosive offense, and they paid the price for it. As usual, I did my best to provide some context to some of the key plays from the game.

You couldn’t ask for better blocking than this from the offensive line, which was great to see after such a poor performance last weekend. To a man, the line drives their assignment out of the hole and provides Isaac Brown more room than any back has seen this year.

A term you hear a lot when it comes to offensive line play is “strain”. Lance Robinson is 5 yards down the field to block a linebacker who is right in the path of this play. His ability to get to this block on time is key to Isaac Brown being able to blow right by him and the backside defender who is closing on this play. This line can get the job done, but they have to do it consistently.

This was the first blown coverage of the game as well as the first of nine NC State completions of 16 or more yards on the day. TJ Banks spent a lot of time on Saturday with his arms out to his side, wondering how the receiver was so wide open. On this play, it’s because Banks let him run past him without carrying him down the field.

I’ll be repeating this a lot, so get used to it. There is no threat in Banks’ area, so he should be getting depth until he stops in the endzone. He provides no value to the defense where he is on the field, and the running back coming out of the backfield will be picked up by Stanquan Clark if needed. Keep in mind, there are only five receivers on any given play. Everyone is accounted for but the guy who catches the ball.

This is a two-by-two vertical route concept which is meant to be a zone-beater. The goal is to put the second-level defenders in conflict, which is exactly what we see. My issue is that you can see it played the right way to the bottom of the screen. TJ Capers carries the receiver down the field (albeit not as well as you’d like) to force what would have to be a very good throw between himself and the safety.

Banks lets his man go into wide-open space, and Bailey has an easy throw to make. If he carries him, the likely option is the check down to the back, which leads to a third down.

Louisville was flat-out bad on third downs Saturday, but for the third straight week, they utilized four pass rushers on third down, and it ended with a failed play for the offense. Micah Carter and Jarod Smith came in the game to play defensive tackle, and they immediately get pressure up the middle, which they have struggled mightily with this season. Smith loops around to land right in CJ Bailey’s lap, and they get a hit on the quarterback.

They can do this on every single third and long, but they just don’t do it. I would love to know why.

It was tough to see Keyjuan Brown distraught on the sideline late in this game, because this is the type of effort he brings every game. The right side of Louisville’s line does a good job of getting push on a play that is designed to run behind them. However, Anwar O’Neal lets his man run right by him because he steps down with the effort I give at work on a Friday at 3 pm. Justyn Reid is forced to run this player out of the play instead of leading Brown through the hole that is created on the right side.

Brown is patient enough to let Reid’s block work before he bursts up the field into the planned path of the play. Because Reid isn’t there to take on the free player at the second level, Brown is forced to make him miss by running through his tackle, while also running through the tackle of the backside safety who is chasing the play. This is all before he makes the frontside safety look silly in the open field. He may have broken this run if he had seen the player who ends up making the tackle a little sooner.

This was one of the best play designs I’ve seen from Jeff Brohm this year. NC State is an aggressive defense with linebackers responsible to fill in run support, so Brohm calls a fake sprint out to the left with a pulling guard and routes crossing to the left side of the field. You can see Tre Richardson going across towards the middle of the field in the clip.

But Richardson actually circles back and breaks towards the sideline while Lincoln Kienholz stops short before he squares up to look for Richardson.

Two things stand out to me about this play that should be pointed out. The running back getting to the flat is a subtle nuance to this play that I love. As he hits the flat, he ensures the flat defender in zone will have to stay short. That clears out plenty of room to make the throw.

The other thing I love on this play is Richardson staying flat on his route because he sees the zone defender, who ends up forcing him out of bounds. As Richardson turned for this route, he identified where the defense was and made sure he was where his quarterback needed him to be. A small thing, but floating even a handful of yards down the field here opens up the opportunity for the defender to make a play on the ball or on Richardson himself.

item.title: NFL officials are calling more penalties than ever
item.description: It’s not your imagination: flags are flying like crazy.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve been feeling like NFL football fields have been awash in yellow this season, your eyes have not deceived you. NFL officials are calling more penalties per game than they have in any season dating back to 2009, and it’s not particularly close.

According to data from NFLPenalties.com, NFL officials are calling a little more than 17 penalties per game this season, the most we’ve seen in any single year since 2009. The average game includes 15 accepted penalties, also the most we’ve seen in any single year in that same time span. The previous highs in both of those categories are 16.2 total flags per game and 13.7 accepted penalties per game, both of which happened in 2015.

The Packers, as you no doubt are aware, are one of the hardest hit teams in this ongoing festival of penalties, averaging 10.5 penalties per game. And for those inclined to say this is a long-term issue for Matt LaFleur’s teams, it really isn’t. Outside of this year, LaFleur’s Packers have typically been right in line with the league average for individual team penalties per game; they’ve never averaged more than 6.2 accepted penalties per game in any season since 2019.

In short, NFL games have been flag fests.

What’s causing the increase? There are a few specific penalties to blame, but it’s all on the offense’s shoulders.

Offensive holding, false start, and delay of game have all seen the biggest increases in per game calls from 2025 to 2026. Holding is being called, on average, 3.13 times per game leaguewide, up from 2.4 per game last year.

We’re seeing 2.78 false start flags per game this year, up from 2.39 last year.

And to round things out, we’ve seen an average of 0.97 delay of game penalties per week, an increase from 0.64 last year.

Those penalties alone don’t account for the increase, though it comes pretty close. But in general, NFL games are seeing more and more penalties; across the 49 different infractions already called at least once this year, 26 are being called at a higher rate than last year. Just 15 are being called at a lower rate.

Generally speaking, if you’re tuning in to watch NFL football this season, chances are good you’re going to see more penalties than ever before.

item.title: Packers LB Edgerrin Cooper expected to miss remainder of season after reportedly tearing his Achilles
item.description: Cooper suffered the injury in Green Bay's Week 4 win over Tampa Bay.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers are expected to be without linebacker Edgerrin Cooper for the remainder of the 2026 season. He was rumored to have torn his Achilles on Sunday, and ESPN's Adam Schefter reported that tests on Monday confirmed the injury.

Cooper missed the end of the Packers' Week 4 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers due to an Achilles injury. After the game, Matt LaFleur said the outlook was "not good" and that they were preparing for him to miss the rest of the season.

The 24-year-old is in his third season. Green Bay selected him in the second round of the 2024 NFL Draft. Cooper played in 14 games as a rookie, making four starts. That year, he had 87 combined tackles, 3.5 sacks and 1 interception. Cooper finished sixth in the Defensive Rookie of the Year voting.

Last year, the linebacker started 16 games and tallied 118 combined tackles. He was credited with only half of a sack but added four passes defended in coverage.

Through four games, Cooper had already tallied 30 tackles, including three sacks, nearly a career-high through the first quarter of the regular season. The linebacker also intercepted a pass and returned it for 18 yards.

Cooper is the latest injury that has hit the Packers. Green Bay has started the season without Micah Parsons, who continues to recover from a torn ACL suffered in 2025.

Wide receiver Jayden Reed suffered a neck injury in Week 2 that required season-ending surgery. Offensive lineman Zach Bako-Bewele will also miss the rest of the season after tearing his right patellar tendon. Backup tight end Luke Musgrave suffered a neck injury in mandatory minicamp, and the team is "hopeful" he can take the field at some point this season.

With Cooper sidelined, the Packers will likely turn to inside linebacker Isaiah McDuffie. He had four tackles in the win and won't fully replicate Cooper's impact, but he should help ensure the loss of one of the foundational pieces on defense doesn't hurt as much.

item.title: Seahawks won’t have Zach Charbonnet, Leonard Williams a maybe versus 49ers
item.description: It’s only Monday, but there will be questions about the running backs and the defensive line for Seattle this week.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday the Seattle Seahawks defeated the Los Angeles Chargers 30-23 at Lumen Field to keep pace with the San Francisco 49ers, who sit alone atop the NFC West at 4-0.

And now comes Week 5 and a matchup against those undefeated 49ers, which means an opportunity for Seattle to take over first place in the division by knocking the Niners out of the top spot.

However, when the teams face off Sunday, the Seahawks will once again be without 2026 first round pick Jadarian Price, who is on injured reserve for at least another three weeks. That brings the discussion to 2023 second round pick Zach Charbonnet and a potential return from injured reserve, but any hopes for that were shot down by head coach Mike Macdonald Monday.

Thus, barring the addition of a veteran free agent, such as Joe Mixon, it appears as though Seattle fans have another week of the former undrafted duo of Emanuel Wilson and George Holani, with Velus Jones seeing situational spot snaps.

However, what could be even more important news on the injury front is the availability of All-Pro defensive lineman Leonard Williams. Williams suffered an ankle injury in the second half against Los Angeles and Macdonald was noncommital regarding Williams’ availability for the showdown against San Francisco.

Williams is a huge piece of the Seattle defense, and while Macdonald says he is optimistic, Macdonald is a dad, and “we will see” more often than not tends to be dad speak for “no.” Should Williams be unable to play against San Francisco it would be a big blow for a defense that has given up far more points than they would prefer the past couple of weeks to opponents of a far lower caliber than the 49ers offense the Seahawks defense will face in Week 5.

And now it’s on to the Wednesday injury report.

item.title: NFL is reviewing two incidents involving officials, including one who appeared to curse at player
item.description: The NFL is looking into two incidents involving confrontations between officials and players during Sunday's games, including one in which a line judge apparently cursed at Arizona's Trey McBride.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL has confirmed that it is looking into two confrontations between officials and players during Sunday’s games, including one in which a line judge was caught on camera apparently cursing at Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride.

Late in the Cardinals’ 36-24 loss to the New York Giants, two- time Pro Bowl selectionMcBride argued a non-call with veteran official Jeff Seeman.. A video of part of the interaction between McBride and Seeman, posted on X by ESPN’s Adam Schefter, appears to show the line judge shouting, “F— you!” at McBride two times.

NFL Players Assn. executive director JC Tretter posted a clip of the interaction that zoomed in on Seeman as he shouted toward McBride.

Read more:Steelers coach Mike McCarthy regrets profane exchange with QB Aaron Rodgers that aired on 'TNF'

“This kind of behavior from an official towards a player is unacceptable,” Tretter wrote. “Players are consistently held accountable when the roles are reversed. We expect the NFL to hold officials to the same standard.”

CBS reporter Aditi Kinkhabwala reposted Tretter’s post and commented that she was “standing right there” during the interaction between McBride and Seeman.

Read more:On hot seat, Jim Harbaugh backs Mike McDaniel again after Chargers fall to 0-4

McBride “was heated for sure, but I never heard a curse from him,” Kinkhabwala wrote. “The harshest he got was, ‘You’re ruining the game.’”

The other incident took place early in the Minnesota Vikings’ 15-10 victory over the Miami Dolphins. On a play that was whistled dead because of a neutral zone infraction, Vikings linebacker Eric Wilson appeared to be shoved into referee Adrian Hill, who was knocked to the ground. When Wilson attempted to help Hill to his feet, the official jumped up and appeared to yell at the player and point for him to move away.

Wilson with the unintentional collision

📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/4HjG8bRF42

— FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) October 4, 2026

“That was funny, honestly,” Wilson told reporters. “I ended up apologizing to him and explained the situation. He was cool about it. He understood what was happening. He just said he was trying to get me — he didn’t want us fighting apparently, me and the Dolphins guy. So he was just trying to break us up.”

Read more:'Our guys found a way.' Rams defy their Philadelphia history in thrilling comeback win

Other than confirming it was looking into both incidents, the NFL had no further comment on the matter. The NFLPA also said it had no further comment on either incident other than Tretter’s X post. The NFL Referees Assn. did not immediately respond on Monday to a request for comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Mack Hollins injury set to open door for more Efton Chism
item.description: Hollins left Sunday’s game in the third quarter.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots saw wide receiver Mack Hollins depart Sunday’s game early with a calf injury. 

While the Patriots await more information to determine the severity of the injury, head coach Mike Vrabel is preparing to potentially be without the veteran in the short term.

“I think we’ll probably know more here in a little bit,” Vrabel said Monday morning. “I don’t know if he’ll be able to practice here for a couple days. But again, I don’t have every detail. I’ll get in there with [the training staff] afterwards and kinda see where we are, and make sure we have guys that are ready to go and everybody is preparing as a starter. We know the energy that Mack brings. The next guy has to be ready to go.”

In Hollins’ absence Sunday, wide receiver Efton Chism III played a season-high 34 offensive snaps in relief. Chism made the most of the opportunity, hauling in two catches for 42 yards and the game-winning touchdown.

The performance could set Chism up for a larger role moving forward.

“Of course. That’s what happens. Guys continue to take advantage of their opportunities, they get more opportunities,” Vrabel said. “We’ve been finding ways to work Chiz in there previously. It’s a balance, but certainly did a lot of things well and I know that he’ll continue to do things well for us and continue to know a bunch of different spots.”

The Patriots are already without A.J. Brown in the wide receiver room, as the veteran remains on injured reserve through at least next week. Hollins’ absence would leave just Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams, and Chism on the active roster.

Undrafted rookies Cameron Dorner and Kyle Dixon, in addition to Chandler Brayboy, are currently on the practice squad.

Vrabel did not rule out the Patriots searching for external additions at the position.

“Sure. Anybody that can help us, we’ll go exploring here shortly,” Vrabel said.

item.title: Explosive plays, special teams miscue Raiders’ undoing in loss to Chiefs
item.description: Kenneth Walker III’s 77-yard gallop, great punch out of ball on kickoff help Kansas City topple Las Vegas 30-27
item.content:encoded:
When CBS Sports play-by-play man Jim Nantz called out Kansas City had generated just 18 total yards of offense with 30 seconds left in the third quarter, it was fortuitous foreshadowing for the Chiefs.

What ensued was an explosive play netting a touchdown and four series later, the visiting Chiefs got another chunk play resulting in another end zone visit. And after punching the ball out of Las Vegas Raiders kick returner Dareke Young, Kansas City found the end zone one play later. Yielding the two explosive plays and the special teams gaffe sunk the home Raiders and the Chiefs reign supreme in the AFC West at 4-0 after a tightly contest 30-27 win this past Sunday.4

What could’ve been a runaway win Kansas City was thwarted by Las Vegas trailing 30-19 in the fourth quarter, but unlike the previous two matchups where takeaways powered the Silver & Black, it was the opposition that showcased more complementary football.

It’s the first defeat for Raiders rookie head coach Klint Kubiak — who proclaimed on the broadcast his team would win the game in a half time interview before the two teams went into the locker rooms at half time — and how his team develops and grows after this stinging loss will say a lot about this team going forward. Especially with his football team having a difficult schedule ahead of them.

As longtime NFL analyst Pete Prisco noted above, this isn’t a fugazi football team and what Kubiak is doing is not fluke. How he and his coaching staff pivot after film review from the loss is something many will be watching closely — under a microscope even.

Because yielding explosive plays on defense while not generating more of their own on offense can’t continue to happen, especially for a tough stretch of upcoming games that feature the New England Patriots (road), Buffalo Bills (home), Los Angeles Rams (home), and New York Jets (road) in the next four games.

Las Vegas will also need to rejuvenate a run game that’s been stymied. Perhaps watching the tape of how Walker carved up the defense will provide not only answers for Rob Leonard’s defense, but Kubiak’s offense?

Immediately after Nantz made note of the lack of offensive production, Walker took the hand off on the 1st-and-10 play from the Chiefs’ 11-yard line sprinted through a gaping hole for a 76-yard run. The reason it wasn’t a home run break away touchdown was because of the hustle from Raiders nickel cornerback Taron Johnson, who ran the tailback down.

Two plays later, quarterback Patrick Mahomes threw a dime to wide open wide receiver Tyquan Thornton to boost the Chiefs momentarily lead to 17-13. But Thornton wasn’t done there as he hauled in a 55-yard dime from Mahomes to set up a go-ahead two-yard touchdown run from Walker, 23-19 Chiefs.

Walker hit pay dirt again after the forced fumble and recovery on the ensuing kick off going around the Raiders defense for a 22-yard score and with 30-19 lead in hand and 3:02 left to play, Kansas City was comfortable.

Kubiak and his Raiders weren’t going to go away quietly and made it a game again after quarterback Kirk Cousins escaped a sack and lofted a 20-yard touchdown to tight end Brock Bowers to slash the deficit to 30-27.

The Las Vegas defense rose to the occasion to force a punt but the Raiders’ last gasp on offense ended with Cousins firing an interception on a play that Kubiak admitted he didn’t get quickly enough to his quarterback, hence its haphazard nature and turnover.

Let’s hit the quick slants as fast as both Walker and Thornton torched the Raiders defense on their respective big-play efforts:

—Losing by three points put Kubiak’s decision to go for it on 4th-and-2 instead of keeping the made field goal on the board in the third quarter under the spotlight. To his credit, the rookie’s aggressive decision is something to be done against the high-powered Chiefs, and Kubiak noted he didn’t regret the decision, just regretted the team couldn’t convert and turned the ball over.

—Bowers and fellow tight end Michael Mayer paced the Raiders air attack with six catches for 86 yards and a touchdown and eight receptions for 82 yards, respectively. Reserve tight end Ian Thomas hauled in the other touchdown — a beauty of a 27-yard pass from Cousins where Kubiak schemed the tight end wide open.

—While the tight ends produced 200 yards and two touchdowns on 16 receptions, the wide receivers didn’t produce as much. Tre Tucker had four grabs for 44 yards while Cody White had two receptions for 32 yards. Jeanty did haul in six passes for 68 yards, but the lack of a standout wideout is glaring.

—In the battle of quality punters, the Chiefs’ southpaw Matt Araiza outperformed the Raiders’ AJ Cole III with five boots for 238 yards and all five landing or downed inside Las Vegas’ 20-yard line. Cole had three punts for 142 yards with only one being downed or landing inside the Chiefs’ 20-yard line.

—Walker’s impressive 2026 season continued as he churned out 177 yards on 22 carries (8.0 yards per carry average) with two touchdowns.

—CBS Sports color analyst and likely future hall of fame defensive end J.J. Watt called out that Crosby was on the sideline during Walker’s long 76-yard run for a breather. And just like Watt noted, giving up that kind of explosive play with your best defender taking a rest likely is the catalyst for Crosby to once again play near 100 percent of snaps.

—In comparison, the Raiders’ entire run game rushed for 72 yards on 26 carries (2.8 yards per carry) with Ashton Jeanty leading the group with 58 yards on 15 carries. Rookie running back Mike Washington Jr. added 18 yards on 9 totes while fullback Connor Heyward had two carries for negative four yards.

Quotes of Note

“I took three points off the board, and we were going to be aggressive going into the game. I don’t regret it. I regret not getting it.”

—Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak on going for it on 4th-and-2 in the third quarter instead of taking the made field goal.

“That’s a good football team. You know they had a few people defensively come over for them. They added to the talent they had. The D line and secondary were playing together. That’s a good team. When Kirk’s dealing like that it’s hard to stop. And they have a guy like Brock Bowers. We have to keep getting better but I’m sure they will do the same.”

—Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes on the Las Vegas Raiders after the win.

Up Next

Las Vegas (3-1) preps for an East Coast trip to face New England (2-2) next Sunday. The Patriots head into Week 5 after a big win over the Buffalo Bills in their AFC East clash. The Raiders are 2-0 on the road so far this season and will need similar strong performances the team had at the Los Angeles Chargers and New Orleans Saints. Unlike the two previous away games, however, this is the first for the Silver & Black that’s an early 10 a.m. (Pacific Standard Time) matchup.

item.title: Report: Rashawn Slater believed to have a high-ankle sprain
item.description: The Chargers saw left tackle Rashawn Slater get hurt in Sunday's loss to the Seahawks and the 0-4 team is reportedly set to be without him for a while.
item.content:encoded:
The Chargers saw left tackle Rashawn Slater get hurt in Sunday's loss to the Seahawks and the 0-4 team is reportedly set to be without him for a while.

Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that the belief is that Slater suffered a high-ankle sprain. He'll have an MRI to confirm that diagnosis and he will likely miss multiple weeks if the team gets that confirmation.

Slater missed all of the 2025 season with a torn patellar tendon and he missed most of the 2022 season with a torn biceps, so the Chargers have experience playing without him.

They were also missing right tackle Joe Alt for most of last season and Alt suffered a neck injury on Sunday, so climbing out of the early hole they've dug themselves this season is not shaping up to be an easy task.

item.title: Tyson Bagent to start for Bears in Week 5 rivalry game vs. Packers
item.description: Tyson Bagent will be under center when the Bears take on the Packers in Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears have won three games so far during the 2026 NFL season, all with a different quarterback leading the charge. With starter Caleb Williams still sidelined due to a hamstring injury, Bears coach Ben Johnson had a tough decision to make ahead of the team's massive rivalry game against the Green Bay Packers in Week 5: Should he start Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent?

Unlike last week, Johnson didn't leave Bears fans in suspense, announcing Bagent would start against the Packers in Week 5.

Tyson Bagent will start for the Bears in Week 5 against the Green Bay Packers, coach Ben Johnson said on his weekly radio hit at ESPN-1000.

— Sean Hammond (@sean_hammond) October 5, 2026

Johnson wasn't so forthcoming heading into Week 4. Following Williams' injury in Week 2, Johnson was forced to turn to Keenum — the team's third-string quarterback — in a Week 3 win over the Philadelphia Eagles due to Bagent overcoming a concussion.

Bagent was able to return to practice, however, opening the door for him to return in Week 4. But after Keenum performed well in Week 3, there were questions over who the Bears would go with against the New York Jets in Week 4.

Johnson refused to outright answer the question, and even trolled those asking once the game started. After news leaked Saturday suggesting Bagent would start, Johnson put both Keenum and Bagent on the field for the game's first play. Both players technically received a start, though Keenum was the one lined up in shotgun. The Bears ran on the play, so Keenum did not accumulate any passing attempts.

From there, Bagent received every snap. He performed admirably, completing 25 of 34 pass attempts for 268 yards and an interception in the team's 23-13 win.

It was a solid game, though not as impressive as Keenum's Week 3 start from a statistical standpoint.

Additionally, Bagent had a few turnover-worthy plays that were called back by penalty. The backup had three interceptions negated by penalty. One of those was a free play where Bagent just threw it up to his receiver. The other two were overturned after the fact, with Bagent potentially unaware that would be the case when he released the ball.

Bagent, however, also had a few moments where he showed a stronger arm and higher upside than Keenum. A downfield strike to Rome Odunze in the middle of the field was not a throw the team asked Keenum to make in Week 3.

Rome Odunze picks up 37!

NYJvsCHI on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/pupC7cnmpB

— NFL (@NFL) October 4, 2026

Due to the stat disparity — and the fact that it's Chicago — Johnson's decision to go with Bagent over Keenum could wind up being contentious locally. Bears fans, unsurprisingly, have a lot of thoughts when it comes to backup quarterbacks. They've had plenty of experience in that arena before.

Unfortunately for Bagent, Johnson and Keenum, all of that escalates when the Bears play the Packers. If Bagent goes out there and leads the team to yet another win, it will be another feather in Johnson's cap.

If not, it could be one of the few times since taking over that Johnson receives criticism from Bears fans.

item.title: Seahawks-Chargers, Words of Prey: NFL completes decades-long transition to flag football
item.description: Seattle sets franchise record for penalty yardage in interminable victory. Always reaching new heights, these guys.
item.content:encoded:
In the last 120 minutes of their young season, we’ve seen the worst the 2026 Seattle Seahawks have to offer. The three turnovers in Washington that sank an offensive renaissance. Then, early defensive domination was undone by untimely mistakes and lack of discipline back at home. Sloppiness in all three phases on critical downs gifted points to opponents in close games, repeatedly.

In their last 120 minutes, more things went wrong than a fan can count, even a Sea-soned Hawks fan, and still Seattle earned a split. Depending on your point of view, that’s either a reason to rejoice or to worry. Ah, who am I kidding — been doing a bit of both myself and I’ll guess you have too. It’s reassuring to be able to win even playing under your talent level. These aren’t the Dolphins or Cardinals, who have basically room for error if they want to post the W.

Speaking of inferior teams, whooping the winless Los Angeles Chargers 30-13 as the fourth quarter begins is usually the recipe for a final quarter of self-congratulations, toasts in the crowd, and everyone in Seahawks Nation looking ahead to a Week 5 clash with the 49ers. Instead, one near-meltdown later, on the heels of stubbing your toe the week prior, the whole enterprise suddenly feels shaky. Seattle converted exactly one third down on the ground, did not sustain drives after building a three-score lead, and did not defend well enough to slam the door well before the final minute, but at least they did that. Uchenna Nwosu provided the capper on a big revenge game (those are real):

LA was in position to win because of Justin Herbert’s excellent second half, implausible toughness, and a veritable plague of personal fouls — seven in total for Seattle. One early soft call on Brady Russell stomped on a drive before it had a chance to bloom. Connor O’Toole drew one for a borderline helmet-to-helmet when the punt returner unwisely declined to make a fair catch. Nick Emmanwori’s inexplicable headbutt with five seconds before half left stopped the clock and put the Chargers in comfortable field goal range. Devon Witherspoon tackled a dude four steps out of bounds, Emmanwori grabbed a facemask in the open field, DeMarcus Lawrence hit Herbert low and Derick Hall hit him late on the same drive. And that’s not counting the offsetting personal fouls somewhere in that first quarter, well before the game descended into a parody of itself.

The 150 yards in penalties were a new franchise record. (More than any Raiders game back in the AFC West days, even.)

Fortunately, the Chargers arrived with an entire case of beers, and at the contest’s most critical moments, they’d casually pull one out and ask the Seahawks to hold it. When Los Angeles was perfectly poised to conduct a proper game-winning drive with all three timeouts, Justin Eboigbe landed on Sam Darnold after his slide, freshening the downs for Seattle and forcing longtime Seahawks sufferer Jim Harbaugh to burn them after all.

There’s a sequence in the third quarter that captures the essence of this flagfest better than any. Do note the expressions on Jason Myers’ and Michael Dickson’s faces — “What are we even doing, guys.” You probably saw these at your watch party, in your row at the stadium, or on your own face at some point Sunday afternoon.

You can watch the video, but just in case you don’t: Greg Zabel isn’t on the field until the play clock hits 10, so he hurries to his assignment. The kick is snapped at zeroes, Myers pushes it right, giving LA excellent field position EXCEPT NO, there’s a late leverage call against the defense, first down Seattle instead. (The drive would end soon thereafter in three points, which seemed superfluous at the time but ended up pretty dang important.)

Anyway. It’s fun to complain about a win, sure beats the alternative. Thirty penalties and countless bullet wounds in everybody’s feet later, the Seahawks had emerged with their third victory of the year. Truly, ‘bout the only surprise is their victory formation went off without a flag. The recap will omit most of the fouls, if possible.

Before we get there! It would be criminal to not mention Emanuel Wilson’s big day. Not by choice entirely, Mike Macdonald and Brian Fleury traded their explosive but risky running attack for a more reliable, albeit boring dose of Wilson and George Holani. It frickin’ worked. (I will never stop quoting Pete Carroll no matter how many Super Bowls [four] Macdonald wins here.)

Wilson rewarded his coaches, teammates and himself with a tough, tough 21-81-1 line and that first-quarter touchdown reception that sent the Chargers chasing the hosts for the rest of the afternoon. Factor in 51 more yards from Rashid Shaheed and Holani and you have the makings of a respectable running game. Which you’ll need.

Q1: Seahawks 7, Chargers 3

Predator: The officiating crew

Prey: Anyone watching

How: We didn’t know it yet, but maybe we should’ve. Like when the officials found offsetting personal fouls that instant replay couldn’t locate. That should’ve alerted viewers. Then, Russell was dinged 15 for this “offense”:

Later, O’Toole’s personal came for leading with the helmet but you can see him pull up. Maybe it’s a flag but that exact hit is performed on every drive and Derius Davis never put his hand up.

I don’t know what a crew can do when a team like the Seahawks repeatedly toes the line with over-aggressiveness some might call dirty. But it was hard to watch the parade of yellow.

Action: In the most mulligan-y of starts conceivable, Herbert and Darnold traded interceptions on successive plays. What to say about that, except you’d like to win the turnover battle from there on out, and the Seahawks did. The Chargers offense settled in first though, with two rapid-fire first downs, one semi-explosive pass play and one questionable offsides against Nwosu to creep into field goal range. An eight-play, 30-yard drive off the pick resulted in three points.

And when Seattle’s real opening possession ended in an awkward intentional grounding, the hangover from that Commander got real rear view mirror-like: objects are closer than they appear.

No matter, O’Toole reached into his special toolebox and pulled out a timely fumble recovery.

The game was barely five minutes old, and each possession was a whiplash. Add Weeks 3 and 4 together and a fan could be forgiven for believing they were watching the 2010s Chaoshawks again. (Recite the Kevin Clark tweet from memory, if you know what I mean.) Yet the pattern of this particular meeting had already manifested: the Chargers were happy to beat themselves, the Seahawks happy to oblige.

Off the giveaway, it took exactly one play for Wilson to tilt the field. Little screen to the right, and with ball in hand he turned and went north-south with more determination than a Blackpoll warbler (safe to Google it, go ahead). Seattle ended up six points richer.

The next seven possessions ended in punts. Emmanwori and Lawrence helped kill drives with tackles for loss, and as the second quarter took off, so did the Seahawks pass rush.

Q2: Seahawks 20, Chargers 6

Predator: Byron Murphy

Prey: Interior linemen, assuming they existed at all

How: Living in the backfield. In the first clip, the literal first snap of the quarter, Murphy lines up three tech but sideswipes the left guard at his opposite shoulder, switching to the A gap. The lineman is helpless and Murph gets home with acceleration. Much like we used to see that one Los Angeles Ram do — you know, the guy who played, then didn’t play, then decided to come back and play, except half the time he still doesn’t.

Next drive, same penetration, more friends join Murphy, it’s a whole party back there.

If you watch to the end you’ll see Murphy turned around between the lineman and Herbert. Basically blocking. So considerate of him.

Action: That Murphy sack forced a punt, which would’ve given Seattle great field position if they hadn’t been flagged for hands to the face. No matter, there were still two punts to get through, and the Seahawks did not waste every opportunity, because they’re a great team even when they’re cosplaying as a mediocre one.

So, six minutes into the second period, an inauspicious Darnold sack and Holani dumpoff seemingly presaged more Michael Dickson. Not so fast. Chat, is it good when even the announcers know your best play? Who cares? I will not matter if that best play is “Jaxon Smith-Njigba reception.”

Three more rushes moved the sticks again, which means play action’s surely next, no that’s a pitch to Shaheed, who follows his blocks, weaves a couple weaves, now the DBs are eating dust, and that quickly Seattle flings six more on the scoreboard. It would remain six only, because Jason Myers’ nice streak of 69 straight made extra points ended. Still, the Seahawks had made it a three-score game in almost no time, a trademark of their Super Bowl-winning ways, and would surely coast to victory. Spoiler: they could’ve coasted a lot more efficiently.

Matching punts took us inside four minutes and to the usual WHEEMAMA, or Weekly HE’s Ernest Moment of Appreciation, Man Alive.

I swear they’re drinking Invisibility Juice at the V-Mac. Or maybe new owner Vinod Khosla has put some proprietary wearable tech on the uniforms that makes them stealthier. Sounds crazy, but never say never.

Wilson punched it in two plays later, making it 14 Seattle points off turnovers, 14 more than the Chargers would earn. Weird how that specific kind of scoring keeps matter week after week, season after season, generation after generation.

So the Chargers, with all of three points and 92 total yards to their name, embarked on a quest to cut the lead before half, and the quest should’ve been quixotic except the Seahawks cleared all the windmills for them. First, Herbert scrambled for 26 yards up the middle on third down and into Seahawks territory. Then, with the clock running under ten seconds, Emmanwori chose that moment to head-butt an opponent, setting up the 39-yarder that closed the gap.

The Seahawks made plenty of stupid mistakes and went into intermission having been flagged nine times. They were fortunate to be out-stupided by a team even more unserious. That’s not likely to happen again and also explains these post-game expressions, which you might again recognize from personal experience. Don’t worry coach, we all watched the same game. We know.

Q3: Seahawks 30, Chargers 13

Predator: Emanuel Wilson

Prey: Bud Dupree

How: Oh, you thought he just scored touchdowns? Then how do you explain this?

Action: The eight-play, 68-yard touchdown drive that the Seahawks assembled out of halftime felt like, in real time, the turning point of this season. You’d scraped by in Week 1 seriously undermanned, rolled to victory in Week 2, received a wake-up call in Week 3, and now you were right again. Everything you wanted to see, made itself visible, in a pleasing chronological order:

  • 31 yard return from Shaheed
  • Immediate strike to JSN for 20
  • First-down run plus defensive holding and you’re at the Chargers 39 almost right away
  • Wilson again powering forward to earn three yards instead of none
  • Darnold reminding everyone how underrated his mobility is with an eight-yard dash to the sideline
  • Cooper Kupp’s first catch to move the sticks again
  • Shaheed gaining five on the play above
  • Wilson setting up third and short with four more;
  • All culminating in confirmation that Tory Horton exists and deserves targets with an easy slant when everyone was expecting run. 27-6.

The drive was exquisite, and good thing, because Seattle would run 16 more offensive plays for a grand total of 37 yards thereafter.

Just as everything looked in order, that’s when things got weird. Last year, as the Dark Side and M.O.B. Ties defense chokeholded opponents to the final whistle, there would seemingly always be that one inexplicable drive where the opposing offense got every break they could collect, all in a row. The kind of that a Madden player might describe as computer f-ckery, where the machine decides it’s gonna score or stop you no matter what. You want to rage-quit, I’ve been there; bit harder to turn the console off in real life though.

The Chargers’ first TD was that drive. A three-yard loss became a first down via penalty on Witherspoon. Emmanwori’s third down stop became another first because of the facemask. Tre Harris got loose for 26 yards, the game’s longest play to that point. The LA offense went backwards again, and surely they wouldn’t escape 3rd and 13, but they did get nine on a nifty swing pass to Oronde Gadsden.

Harbaugh decides the FG does him no good, and there’s only four yards to go besides. Spoon breaks up the pass intended for Gadsden over the middle, the ball bounces straight up instead of the down or to the side, directly into the juggling hands of the young tight end, who falls on his back at the marker. First and goal, takes them two plays to punch it in.

It was a touchdown straight out of the Improbability Drive but it also isn’t rocket science: give teams additional chances on additional drives and they will score extra points. Those are NFL players on the other sideline too. Give them twelve bites at the apple at your own risk.

The Chargers ran a total of 28 offensive plays on their first nine drives combined, then 35 on their next three. Make all the jokes you want about Mike McDaniel’s capris, but he’s getting paid to run an offense and he can do it.

Seattle’s answer looked to be feeble when Myers missed from 53 yards, only to have that infamous leverage penalty give the hosts a second chance. After a whole afternoon of the Chargers’ best play being “run around and wait for the Seahawks to give you 15 yards whether you deserve it or not,” turnabout felt like fair play. The drive soon stalled when Darnold threw into double coverage on third down and JSN couldn’t quite reel it in. All said and done, Myers knocked one through for three redemption points that make it a three possession game again.

The quarter ended with Los Angeles on the move again.

Q4: Seahawks 30, Chargers 20

Predator: Justin Herbert

Prey: Humans not built out of titanium

How: The thing about prey is in the wild, you gotta kill it or it’s not even prey at all, right? Who’s the predator, if the prey survives every attack? Here are two plays Herbert uncorked after being pummeled by Lawrence low and Hall roughing him. On the same drive, even.

Statistically, you’d say the Chargers quarterback figured out how to prey on the Seahawks defense. After all,

Herbert, before half: 5-14-36-0-2.

Herbert, after half: 14-18-153-1-0.

For one possession, Herbert was the apex predator. Clever, evasive, versatile, bigger and tougher. Plus, unkillable. He got hit four times on the touchdown drive that spanned quarters. Trey Lance put on the armband but never got a chance to come in. He survived two roughing calls, a legit sack, a collision with Drake Thomas, and put his head down for three yards inside the five on a designed QB run.

Of course, Nwosu’s last-minute clincher and Hall’s timely surehandedness rendered Herbert’s heroics moot in terms of result. They still happened.

Action: LA did paydirt for the second time in as many drives, the lead did shrink to ten, but the 8:31 they expended probably suited Macdonald just fine. All Seattle needed was to burn a little clock of their own (check, 3:47 before punting), not give up a touchdown (check, it was a field goal after a defensive breakdown I’ll mention later), possess the ball past the two minute warning (check, with help), and bring the house until time expired. Check on that too.

It wasn’t a very satisfying way to get back in the win column. Does that matter? Not in the standings. Through four games, you’d like to have seen more than mere glimpses of the disciplined special teams, controlled violence on defense, and explosive offense on both ground and air that got the Hawks all the way last season. All we’ve had are glimpses and it’ll take more than that to approach last year’s success. Which was a Super Bowl title. The Seahawks are defending champs. Of the NFL. Right now, even. And 3-1. Without having played their best ball, even. Just, could we have a bit more, please?

Morning Preyers

Let’s not overdo this.

Nick Emmawori’s sack that set the Chargers back 15 yards in the fourth quarter was a thing of beauty. His tackle where he caught a half-second too much facemask was too. He’s healthy and one of the few guys in the league who deserves to be called a force multiplier.

Seattle’s pass rush is so good even without E-Man. But he’s almost impossible to contain because he’ll play positionaless football. How can you know where he’ll line up next? Mike Macdonald, man.

Loved to see (late in the fourth) Drake Thomas blow up a screen in the backfield, an effort that could’ve been pivotal had the Chargers not converted fourth and seven to midfield on the very next snap. I give Thomas 0.9 KJ’s on the play for his trouble.

Speaking of that, it’s still mystifying to me that Quentin Johnston didn’t have two men draped all over him downfield, and that Rodney Thomas arrived late. Johnston was fair game to bump around, Herbert was way out of the pocket. Too many things in this victory smelled like the good old bad old Seahawks, who took years off everyone’s lives while seemingly enjoying it.

This game was partially won by the defense with their relentless harassment of Herbert, but it would’ve been way smoother with some relenting on that harassment when he was in the pocket. Lawrence was stumbling toward Herbert but he still went low. Hall didn’t need to try and knock Herbert out of the game for good with a pretty late hit. Those are plays other fans will describe as dirty, and I won’t argue.

Safe to say that one doesn’t go in the rewatch vault.

The Commanders and Chargers are 1-7 combined. The lone win came against Seattle. It was good to prevail against the Cardinals and Patriots, but they aren’t anything special. It only gets tougher from here, and the Seahawks didn’t look like a team ready to beat another complete team. Which they haven’t. The first contender to grace their schedule does so in Week 5.

Seattle reaped the reward for fielding a reliable but boring rushing attack over its explosive but risky sibling; will it be enough against the 49ers, who lead the division and the NFL in DVOA? (Because heaven forbid that the Rams’ slow start should make the NFC West any more manageable.)

item.title: Jim Harbaugh not firing Mike McDaniel, remains lone person hopeful about Chargers
item.description: Jim Harbaugh said Mike McDaniel's job is not in jeopardy despite the Chargers' 0-4 start and offensive issues.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Chargers aren't a good team right now. The good or bad news, depending on your opinion of resident offensive coordinators, is that there will be no changes as pertains to Mike McDaniel.

That's the word from head coach Jim Harbaugh, who Saturday had to deal with another loss on the season and yet another moment of doubt placed on this team and its offense.

"His job is not in jeopardy," Harbaugh said of McDaniel, following the Chargers' 30-23 loss Sunday to the Seattle Seahawks. "He's a skilled coach, and we're going to keep growing."

Los Angeles falls to 0-4 on the season, in a division quickly falling into the hands of the Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders. It's a long season, but it feels even longer when you consider how out of sync this Chargers squad has been.

Quarterback Justin Herbert spent some of his day again throwing the ball into the hands of the opposing team, finishing Sunday with two interceptions and one touchdown on 19-for-31 passing for 189 yards.

At the very least, Herbert didn't take long to stifle any notions of an offensive surge, tempering expectations immediately on Sunday with a pick thrown to Seattle's Drake Thomas less than a minute into the game.

Chargers' offensive struggles under Mike McDaniel

Mike McDaniel's creative and oftentimes complex strategy isn't exactly hitting on any cylinders at the start of the season.

The stats don't lend much in the way of celebration four games in: 16.8 points per game (No. 29), 185.3 passing yards/game (No. 24), 38 offensive penalties (No. 4) and fifth in the league in percentage of drives ending in an offensive turnover (19.1).

There is little respite as L.A. next welcomes division rival the Denver Broncos to SoFi this coming week.

For his part, Harbaugh sounds hopeful.

"The plan did not work to result in a victory, and we'll go back and plan some more with the skilled coaches we have and the talented players and fight," Harbaugh said on Sunday. "That's what gives me optimism."

That gives us at least one person in Los Angeles who is optimistic about the Chargers.
